prompt: In the first phase, `arrivalRate: 1` and `rampTo: 3` over `duration: 5`. What happens?

choices.text: New visitors arrive at a rate rising from 1 to 3 a second over 5 seconds
choices.why: Right. Each visitor runs the flow once and leaves.

choices.text: Three visitors loop over the flow for 5 seconds, each starting again when it ends
choices.why: That would be a closed model; Artillery's phases count arrivals.

choices.text: One request a second, then three
choices.why: The rate is of visitors, and each sends two requests.

choices.text: The test waits through 5 seconds of warm-up before the first visitor arrives
choices.why: The phase is load from its first second.

prompt: What does the `capture` under the first `get` do for the booking that follows?
hint: `$.id` is a path into the answer.

choices.text: It saves the whole answer to a file for the report
choices.why: Nothing is written to a file; the value goes into a variable.

choices.text: It puts the answer's `id` into `show`
choices.why: Right. `{{ show }}` in the POST is that captured value.

choices.text: It checks that the answer was a 200
choices.why: Capturing reads a value; it asserts nothing about the status.

choices.text: It records the response time under the name `show`
choices.why: Times are recorded for every request anyway; `capture` reads the body.

prompt: In an Artillery scenario, the 95th percentile limit and `maxErrorRate` sit under the key ___ inside `config`.
hint: The plugin named just above it.

prompt: A journey needs a booking body computed from a list of seats the test reads at start-up. Where does that logic go in Artillery?

choices.text: Into the YAML, as a loop under `flow`
choices.why: YAML has no way to compute a body; that is where it runs out.

choices.text: A JavaScript file named in `config.processor`
choices.why: Right. The test then becomes two files in two languages.

choices.text: Into a second YAML file under `phases`
choices.why: Phases decide arrivals, not request bodies.

choices.text: Nowhere, since Artillery sends bodies exactly as written
choices.why: It can, through a processor function.

prompt: Every booking starts answering 500, and the scenario is unchanged. What does the `Checks` block of the Artillery run say?
hint: What does Artillery call an error?

choices.text: `fail: maxErrorRate < 1`, because half the requests failed
choices.why: A 500 is an answer, and Artillery's errors are requests with no answer.

choices.text: Both checks `ok`, with the 500s visible only under `http.codes.500`
choices.why: Right. A rule about status codes has to be written into `ensure` on its own.

choices.text: `fail` on the 95th percentile, because a 500 is slow
choices.why: A 500 is often fast; nothing ties it to the time rule.

choices.text: No `Checks` block at all
choices.why: The block is printed whenever `ensure` is in the file.

prompt: The summary says `http.requests: 112`, and each visitor's flow sends one GET and one POST. How many visitors completed the journey?
What does `--overrides` do in `artillery run boxoffice.yml --overrides '{…}'`?

choices.text: Replaces part of `config` for this run, from JSON on the command line
choices.why: Right. The p95 rule became 5 ms without touching the YAML.

choices.text: Runs the scenario twice and keeps the second result
choices.why: It changes the configuration, and the run happens once.

choices.text: Writes the report to a JSON file
choices.why: That is `--output`.

choices.text: Skips the checks in `ensure`
choices.why: The checks ran, and one of them failed.

prompt: What does `tee results.bin` add to `vegeta attack … | vegeta report`?
hint: Look at the next command in the lesson.

choices.text: It makes the attack faster
choices.why: It copies the stream; the attack runs the same.

choices.text: It turns the binary results into text
choices.why: The file holds the same binary results `report` reads.

choices.text: A copy to report again later, in any form, with nothing sent
choices.why: Right. The histogram was made from that file.

choices.text: It sends the requests to a second server
choices.why: It writes to a file; nothing is sent anywhere.

prompt: At `-rate=300` the report says `rate 300.16` and `throughput 135.39`. What does the gap mean?

choices.text: Vegeta could not send faster than 135 a second
choices.why: It sent at 300.16; the rate column says so.

choices.text: The box office answered fewer than were sent, and the rest waited or timed out
choices.why: Right. An open generator keeps sending, so the backlog shows up in the times.

choices.text: Half the requests were cached
choices.why: Nothing here caches; every answer came from the box office.

choices.text: Vegeta drops the requests it fails to send on time and leaves them out of the rate
choices.why: It starts more workers to keep the rate; nothing was dropped.

prompt: Put the steps of the lesson's Vegeta pipeline in the order the data flows.
hint: From what to send to what came back.
items: vegeta attack sends at the rate
tee keeps a copy of the results

prompt: Vegeta's `Latencies` line reads `[min, mean, 50, 90, 95, 99, max]`. Which value holds lesson 1's requirement?

choices.text: The second, the mean
choices.why: The requirement names a percentile, not the mean.

choices.text: The fifth, the 95th percentile
choices.why: Right. 60.875 ms in the run at 50 a second.

choices.text: The last, the maximum
choices.why: The maximum is one request; the requirement is about 95 in 100.

choices.text: The third, the median
choices.why: The median is the 50th percentile; the requirement asks for the 95th.

prompt: Which of these are true of Vegeta as the lesson runs it? Choose every one that applies.
hint: An attack is a rate and a duration.

choices.text: It keeps sending at the rate even when answers are slow
choices.why: Right. It starts more workers to hold the rate.

choices.text: It has no think time and no notion of a user
choices.why: Right. There are targets, a rate and a duration.

choices.text: Its users wait for each answer before the next request
choices.why: That is a closed model, and Vegeta has no users.

choices.text: A crossed threshold makes `vegeta attack` exit with a non-zero code
choices.why: Vegeta has no thresholds; a script around the report has to decide.

prompt: Which of the six tools has no built-in way to turn a percentile limit into a failed run?
hint: Look at the last column of the table.

choices.text: k6
choices.why: k6 has `thresholds` and exits with 99.

choices.text: Artillery
choices.why: Artillery has `ensure` and exits with 1.

choices.text: Gatling
choices.why: Gatling has `assertions`, and the build fails.

choices.text: Vegeta
choices.why: Right. Its report is read, or parsed by a script that decides.

prompt: A requirement says "200 people with the booking page open, each acting every few seconds". Which pair of tools writes that load most directly?
hint: People inside at once, not arrivals a second.

choices.text: Vegeta and Artillery
choices.why: Both write arrivals a second: an open model.

choices.text: Gatling's `injectOpen` and k6's arrival rate
choices.why: Both count arrivals, not people inside.

choices.text: Locust and JMeter
choices.why: Right. Both model users that loop with a wait: a closed model.

choices.text: Vegeta and Gatling's `injectOpen`
choices.why: Both keep a rate whatever the server does.

choices.text: Locust for the journey, and Vegeta with a script that reads its report for the rate
choices.why: Right. Python the team reads, and an open tool for a question stated as a rate.

choices.text: Vegeta for both
choices.why: Vegeta has no journeys: no flow, no capture, no think time.

choices.text: Gatling for the journey and Locust for the rate
choices.why: A Java test on a Python team, and a closed tool for an open question.

prompt: Against the same box office, Vegeta at 300 a second reports a median of 2.413 s, while a closed tool with 10 looping users reports a median near 60 ms. Which number describes visitors who arrive 300 a second?
hint: Who kept arriving while the box office was behind?

choices.text: The closed tool's, because its ten users measured each answer carefully
choices.why: It measured what its ten users met, and they slowed down with the server.

choices.text: Neither, since the two disagree
choices.why: They answer different questions; one of them is this one.

choices.text: The average of the two
choices.why: Averaging a rate question with a users question describes no load at all.

choices.text: Vegeta's, because it kept sending at the rate and timed the waiting
choices.why: Right. Visitors who arrive regardless wait in line, and only the open run counted that.

prompt: A colleague adds Vegeta to the pipeline as `echo … | vegeta attack -rate=50 -duration=60s | vegeta report`, and the job is green on a day the 95th percentile reached 900 ms. Why?

choices.text: No step compares the numbers with a limit, so the exit code stays 0
choices.why: Right. A step has to read the report, for example with `-type=json` and `jq`, and exit non-zero.

choices.text: Sixty seconds is too short a run for Vegeta to collect a 95th percentile at all
choices.why: The time was measured; nobody judged it.

choices.text: Vegeta drops slow requests from its report
choices.why: Slow answers are in the percentiles; timeouts are in the error set.

choices.text: The pipeline reads only the last line
choices.why: The pipeline reads the exit code, and it was 0.
